== sources/ostrich-benchmark-2026.md
# Ostrich 0.9 compression benchmark (project wiki, March 2026)

Ostrich compressed our sample of application text logs 4.1 times on average (zstd level 3: 3.2 times), at 410 MB/s
on one core.

Scope: the sample held 2,000 text log files, each under 1 MB. Binary payloads, files over 1 MB and multi-core runs
were not tested, so these numbers say nothing about them.
== sources/ostrich-readme.md
# Ostrich

Ostrich is a dictionary compressor for small text records. It trains a dictionary per stream (`ostrich train`) and
needs the same dictionary to decompress.

final.result:
**Probably not, and nothing in ./sources supports it.**

- **Wrong kind of data.** The README says Ostrich is a dictionary compressor built for small text records. Your archives are protobuf binary frames, 40–300 MB per file.
- **The benchmark doesn't cover your case.** The March 2026 wiki result (4.1× vs zstd‑3's 3.2×, at 410 MB/s on one core) came from text logs under 1 MB each. It says itself that binary payloads, files over 1 MB and multi-core runs weren't tested.
- **Extra work to run it.** Ostrich trains a dictionary per stream, and you need that same dictionary to decompress. You'd have to store and version the dictionaries for as long as you keep the archives.

If you still want to consider it, run it against zstd on a few real nightly files first. Until then, zstd (maybe with `--long` for large files) is the safer default. That last part is my suggestion; the sources don't cover it.

I saved both source findings to the research shelf in memory.
